note: A safe lane change requires checking mirrors, signaling, and checking blind spots and surrounding traffic, including other vehicles that may also be moving into the same lane. What you must avoid is changing lanes without these checks or signals, because that greatly increases the risk of a collision with a vehicle you did not see.

question: While waiting to turn left at an intersection, you should:
options: a: Signal and keep wheels turned left, b: Signal and keep wheels straight, c: Flash headlights to clear traffic
note: When waiting to turn left, signal your turn and keep your wheels straight. If another vehicle hits you from behind, straight wheels help prevent your car from being pushed into oncoming traffic.

question: When may you pass with a solid and broken yellow line if the broken line is on your side?
options: a: Only in an emergency.,b: On an expressway.,c: If traffic is clear.
note: A solid and broken yellow line together means passing is allowed only on the side with the broken line. If the broken line is on your side, you may pass when traffic is clear and it is safe, and you can complete the pass without interfering with oncoming vehicles.

question: On a multilane road with opposing traffic, the shared center lane is for:
options: a: Passing another vehicle, b: Slowing or stopping before a left turn, c: Through-traffic when moving slowly
note: On roads with a shared center left‑turn lane, that lane is used only for vehicles preparing to turn left (or for permitted U‑turns), not for passing or for driving straight ahead. You may briefly enter it to slow or stop while waiting for a safe gap to turn.

question: What should you do when passing other vehicles?
options: a: Check mirrors and blind spots.,b: Honk three times.,c: Re-enter within 10 feet of the passed vehicle.
note: Before passing, you must check your mirrors and blind spots, signal, move into the passing lane, and pass safely at a legal speed. Return to your lane only when you can see the entire front of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror and there is enough space. Honking repeatedly or cutting back in too close is unsafe and not required.

question: How can you check your blind spots when changing lanes?
options: a: Use the inside rearview mirror.,b: Use the outside rearview mirror.,c: Use both rearview mirrors.,d: Turn your head and quickly glance over your shoulder in the direction you want to move.
note: Mirrors alone cannot show you everything around your vehicle. Each vehicle has blind spots—areas to the sides and slightly behind you that do not appear in either the inside or outside mirrors. To safely change lanes, you must first check your mirrors, then quickly turn your head and glance over your shoulder in the direction you plan to move to be sure no vehicle is in your blind spot.

question: What must you do before changing lanes?
options: a: Signal your intent early.,b: Check your blind spot.,c: Ensure the lane is clear.,d: All of the above.
note: Before changing lanes, you must signal in advance, check your mirrors, and look over your shoulder to check your blind spot, then move only when the lane is clear. All three actions are required for a safe lane change, not just ensuring the lane is clear.

question: When should you return to your lane after passing?
options: a: When you can see the front of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.,b: When the other driver signals you.,c: When directly next to the passed vehicle.
note: After passing, do not return to your lane just when you "feel" far enough ahead or when you are still next to the other vehicle. Stay in the passing lane until you can see the entire front of the vehicle you passed in your inside rearview mirror, then signal and move back when it is safe.

question: When may you not cross a single broken white or yellow line?
options: a: If it interferes with traffic.,b: When turning left into a driveway.,c: When the car ahead is disabled.
note: A single broken white or yellow line means you may cross it to pass or turn when it is safe and legal. You must not cross if doing so would interfere with oncoming or adjacent traffic—for example, if you would force other drivers to slow or swerve.

question: What type of line allows passing another vehicle?
options: a: Broken white.,b: Double solid yellow.,c: Solid yellow.
note: Broken white lines separate lanes of traffic moving in the same direction and allow lane changes and passing when it is safe. Solid yellow or double solid yellow lines generally mean no passing across them.

question: Which statement about passing is true?
options: a: Signal 100 feet before passing, b: Check mirrors and left shoulder blind spot, c: Wait to see both headlights of the passed vehicle before returning, d: All of the above
note: Safe passing involves several coordinated steps: signal well in advance (at least 100 feet before changing lanes in most areas), check your mirrors and your blind spot over the left shoulder to be sure the lane is clear, pass promptly without speeding excessively, and do not move back into your original lane until you can see both headlights of the vehicle you passed in your rearview mirror.

question: What should you do when passing a large truck?
options: a: Re-enter your lane and slow down immediately.,b: Give the truck ample space before re-entering.,c: Re-enter whenever you choose.
note: When passing a large truck, stay in the passing lane until you can see the entire front of the truck (including its headlights) in your rearview mirror. This ensures you have fully cleared the truck’s longer stopping distance and blind spots. Re-enter your lane smoothly and maintain your speed so you do not force the truck to brake suddenly.

question: A driver may legally pass on the right of another vehicle:
options: a: If the vehicle is waiting to turn left and a passing lane is available, b: Even if it requires driving off the pavement, c: On a narrow bridge
note: You may pass on the right only when it can be done safely and without leaving the paved roadway, such as when the other vehicle is turning left and there is a clearly marked lane for you to use, or on roads with two or more lanes in your direction. You must never drive off the pavement or onto the shoulder to pass.

question: You may not pass within ____ of a bridge, viaduct, or tunnel.
options: a: 200 feet, b: 100 feet, c: 500 feet
note: You may not pass within 100 feet of a bridge, viaduct, or tunnel because your view of oncoming traffic can be blocked and there is often no room to escape if something goes wrong. Staying in your lane in these areas reduces the risk of head‑on collisions.

question: How should drivers use a shared center lane on a multilane road with opposing traffic?
options: a: To pass another vehicle.,b: To slow or stop before turning left.,c: As a through-traffic lane.
note: On roads with a shared center left‑turn lane, that lane is only for vehicles preparing to turn left from either direction. You may use it to slow or stop while waiting for a safe gap to turn, but you must not use it to pass other vehicles or as a regular travel lane.

question: When another driver attempts to pass your vehicle, you should:
options: a: Pull off the road, b: Signal when it’s safe for them to pass, c: Maintain or slightly reduce speed and stay in your lane to allow safe passing
note: When another driver is passing you, you should help them pass safely by maintaining a steady speed or slightly reducing speed and staying in your lane. You should not signal for them or judge gaps for them; each driver is responsible for deciding when it is safe to pass. Your main job is to avoid speeding up and to allow enough space for the passing vehicle to return to the lane safely.

question: On a multilane highway, to move from the right lane to the left, you should:
options: a: Check rearview mirror for traffic behind, b: Check left shoulder for blind spot, c: Check side mirror and signal, d: All of the above
note: Before moving from the right lane to the left on a multilane highway, check your rearview mirror for traffic behind, check your left side mirror, signal your intention, and look over your left shoulder to check your blind spot. Only change lanes when it is safe and clear.

question: Before making a left turn, it’s critical to:
options: a: Sound your horn, b: Yield to oncoming traffic, c: Swing to the right side of your lane
note: When turning left, you must yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians because they have the right-of-way unless you have a protected green arrow. You should wait until it is safe and clear before turning. Sounding your horn is rarely required, and swinging right in your lane before turning left is unsafe and can confuse other drivers.

question: You may not park:
options: a: On a hill.,b: In a parking lot.,c: On a crosswalk or bike lane.
note: You must not park on a crosswalk or in a bike lane because these areas are reserved for pedestrians and cyclists. Blocking them forces people into traffic and creates serious safety risks. Always leave crosswalks and bike lanes completely clear.

question: Emergency vehicles:
options: a: Have right-of-way with sirens or flashing lights, b: May use loudspeakers for instructions, c: May travel in groups, d: All of the above
note: When an emergency vehicle approaches with its lights and siren on, it has the right-of-way and you must yield, usually by pulling to the right and stopping. Emergency vehicles may use loudspeakers to give drivers specific instructions, and they often travel in groups, so you should look and listen for more than one vehicle before proceeding.

question: Drivers may not park within ____ of a railroad crossing.
options: a: 50 feet, b: 65 feet, c: 100 feet
note: You may not park within 50 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing. This keeps the area clear so drivers and pedestrians can see approaching trains and so trains have room to pass safely.

question: You may drive in the HOV lane if:
options: a: Your vehicle has at least the minimum number of occupants shown on the HOV signs (often two or more), b: You’re driving slower than traffic, c: You’re driving faster than traffic
note: High‑Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) lanes are generally reserved for vehicles carrying at least the minimum number of occupants shown on the signs, often two or more people. You must also obey any posted time restrictions and special rules for motorcycles, buses, or clean‑air vehicles, which may be allowed even with a single occupant if signs permit.

question: Drivers may deposit litter while on roadways:
options: a: In designated litter barrels, b: In the median, c: In ditches
note: You must never throw litter onto the road, shoulder, median, or ditches. Litter may only be placed in proper containers, such as designated litter barrels or trash cans at rest areas or other marked locations. This keeps roads safe and clean and avoids fines for littering.

question: When parallel parking between two cars, what should you do first?
options: a: Turn wheels to the left.,b: Turn wheels to the right.,c: Pull up even with the car in front.
note: To begin parallel parking, first pull up alongside and even with the car in front of the space, leaving a safe gap. Then check traffic, signal, and start backing into the space while turning the wheel as needed.

question: Drivers may not park within ____ of a crosswalk.
options: a: 20 feet, b: 30 feet, c: 35 feet
note: You may not park within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection. This space must be kept clear so drivers and pedestrians can see each other and have time to react, reducing the risk of collisions.

question: What should you do when leaving a parking space?
options: a: Check for children and obstacles.,b: Signal to other drivers.,c: Check your mirrors.,d: All of the above.
note: Before pulling out of a parking space, you must check carefully around your vehicle for children, pedestrians, and obstacles, check your mirrors and blind spots, and signal to alert other drivers of your intention to move. Using all of these steps together helps prevent collisions when re‑entering traffic.

question: When is it acceptable to park in a striped area next to a disabled parking spot?
options: a: Never., b: With a disability plate or placard., c: When all other spaces are full.
note: The striped area next to a disabled parking space is an access aisle, reserved for wheelchair lifts and space for people with disabilities to enter and exit vehicles safely. It is illegal to park or stop in this striped area at any time, even if you have a disability plate or placard or the lot is full.

question: What should you do if an intersection is blocked by traffic?
options: a: Move slowly until traffic clears.,b: Get close to the car in front.,c: Stay out of the intersection.
note: You must not enter an intersection unless you can completely clear it. If traffic is backed up and you would be stuck in the middle when the light changes, stay behind the stop line until there is enough space to drive all the way through.

question: What should you do if you hear a siren but can’t see the emergency vehicle?
options: a: Keep driving until you see it.,b: Pull to the curb and stop.,c: Slow down and don’t stop until you see it.
note: If you hear a siren and think an emergency vehicle may be approaching, safely pull over to the right side of the road and stop. Stay stopped until you are sure the emergency vehicle has passed or is not coming toward you.

question: When parking downhill on a two-way street, what should you do?
options: a: Turn wheels to the right.,b: Turn wheels to the left.,c: Keep wheels straight.
note: When parking downhill on a two-way street with a curb, turn your front wheels toward the curb (to the right). If the vehicle rolls, the front tire will rest against the curb and the car will roll away from moving traffic. Always set the parking brake as well.

question: When must you stop for a school bus?
options: a: When it’s parked with no one inside.,b: When it approaches without flashing lights.,c: On a two-lane road with flashing red lights.
note: On a two-lane road, traffic in both directions must stop when a school bus has flashing red lights and, usually, an extended stop arm. You must remain stopped until the lights stop flashing and the stop arm is withdrawn, because children may be crossing the road.

question: You should not park within ____ of a traffic control signal.
options: a: 50 feet, b: 30 feet, c: 35 feet
note: You must not park within 30 feet of a traffic control signal. Parking too close can block other drivers from seeing the signal and creates a safety hazard at intersections.

question: When stopped on an incline, you should:
options: a: Leave extra space in front of your vehicle, b: Stop at an intersection, c: Stop at a stop sign
note: When stopped on an uphill grade, you should leave extra space in front of your vehicle. If the vehicle ahead rolls backward when starting, that extra space helps prevent a rear-end collision. You should also be ready to brake and, when parked on a hill, turn your wheels and set the parking brake as required by law.

question: How far must your parked vehicle be visible from in each direction?
options: a: 100 feet.,b: 50 feet.,c: 200 feet.
note: Many states require that a parked vehicle on a roadway be visible for at least 200 feet in each direction so other drivers have enough time to see it and react. Parking where your vehicle cannot be seen from a sufficient distance can create a serious hazard, especially on hills or curves.

question: Can you park across from a fire station entrance?
options: a: Yes, if emergency vehicles have left.,b: Yes, at night.,c: No, you must not park directly across from a fire station entrance where it could interfere with emergency vehicles.
note: You may not park directly across from a fire station entrance because emergency vehicles need a clear path to enter and exit quickly. Many states set a specific minimum distance (for example, 75 feet in some jurisdictions), but the key rule is that you must not park in a way that could block or slow emergency vehicles leaving or returning to the station.

question: How close may you not park to an intersection?
options: a: 20 feet.,b: 30 feet.,c: 35 feet.
note: Many states prohibit parking within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, but the exact distance can vary by state law and by whether there is a marked crosswalk or traffic signal. Always check your state’s driver handbook for the specific minimum distance where you live, and never park where you block visibility for drivers or pedestrians.

question: When may you leave your vehicle unattended with the engine running?
options: a: For a brief period.,b: Never.,c: Near a railroad crossing.
note: It is illegal to leave a vehicle idling unattended without turning off the engine and securing it, except with a remote starter.

question: What should you do when you hear or see an emergency vehicle approaching?
options: a: Stop immediately.,b: Drive to the right and stop.,c: Proceed slowly to let it pass.
note: When you see or hear an emergency vehicle using its siren and/or flashing lights, you must yield the right-of-way by pulling as close as safely possible to the right edge of the road and stopping. Do not stop in an intersection; clear the intersection first, then pull over and stop until the emergency vehicle has passed.

question: How close may you not park to a traffic control signal?
options: a: 50 feet.,b: 30 feet.,c: 35 feet.
note: Do not park within 30 feet of a traffic control signal to avoid obstructing visibility and causing crashes.

question: What must you do when an emergency vehicle with sirens or lights approaches?
options: a: Slow down until it passes.,b: Drive to the right and stop.,c: Motion for it to pass.
note: When an emergency vehicle approaches with lights and siren on, you must yield the right‑of‑way by pulling as far to the right side of the road as possible and stopping. Stay stopped until the emergency vehicle has passed, unless a police officer directs you otherwise.

question: What should you do when passing a stopped emergency vehicle?
options: a: Increase speed.,b: Vacate the closest lane or slow down.,c: Ask if help is needed.
note: Move to a lane away from a stopped emergency vehicle or slow down if unable to change lanes, giving it space.

question: Can you park on a freeway shoulder?
options: a: With four-way flashers on.,b: Only in emergencies.,c: To check a map.
note: You may only stop or park on a freeway shoulder in an emergency, such as a breakdown or medical issue. Using your flashers or checking a map is not a valid reason to park there, because stopped vehicles on high‑speed roads create a serious hazard.

question: When may you drive in an HOV lane?
options: a: When your vehicle meets the minimum occupancy shown on the HOV signs (for example, two or more occupants).,b: Whenever you are driving slower than traffic.,c: Whenever you are driving faster than traffic.
note: High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) lanes are reserved for vehicles that meet the minimum occupancy shown on the signs, often two or more people per vehicle. You must follow the posted HOV rules; speed relative to other traffic does not give you permission to use the lane.

question: A 'No stopping' sign indicates that, unless instructed by a police officer, you may stop only:
options: a: To unload packages briefly, b: To avoid interfering with other traffic, c: To drop off passengers
note: A 'No stopping' sign means you may not stop your vehicle at the curb or on the roadway for any reason except when required by traffic conditions, traffic signals, or a police officer. You may not stop to load or unload passengers or goods.

question: Where may you not park?
options: a: On a hill.,b: In a parking lot.,c: On a crosswalk or bike lane.
note: Parking on a crosswalk or in a marked bike lane is illegal because it blocks pedestrians and cyclists and forces them into traffic. Parking on a hill or in a parking lot is allowed as long as you follow posted signs and use proper parking techniques.

question: Drivers may not park within ____ of a fire hydrant.
options: a: 40 feet, b: 25 feet, c: 15 feet
note: You must not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant so firefighters can quickly connect hoses and access water in an emergency. Even if the hydrant is on private property or appears unused, keep at least 15 feet of space clear.

question: You may park or stop on a freeway shoulder:
options: a: With emergency flashers on, b: Only in emergencies, c: To check a map
note: Stopping or parking on a freeway shoulder is generally illegal except for true emergencies, such as a breakdown or medical issue. If you must stop, pull completely off the roadway and use hazard lights so other drivers can see you.

question: When parallel parking, how close should you park to the curb?
options: a: Within 10 inches.,b: Within 12 inches.,c: Within 18 inches.
note: In most U.S. states, you must parallel park with your right-side wheels within about 12 inches (one foot) of the curb. Parking too far from the curb can obstruct traffic and increase the risk of your vehicle being sideswiped. Always check your state handbook, but 12 inches is the standard test-rule distance.

question: A 'No standing' sign at a specific location indicates:
options: a: No stopping allowed at any time, b: Parking is permitted if the driver stays in the vehicle, c: Brief stops are allowed to pick up or drop off passengers
note: A 'No standing' sign means you may stop only briefly to pick up or drop off passengers, but you may not wait there, load or unload cargo, or park the vehicle. If you need to remain stopped longer than the time needed for passengers to get in or out, you must find a legal parking area.

question: Where may you deposit litter while on the roadway?
options: a: In designated litter barrels.,b: In the median.,c: In ditches.
note: Litter must only be placed in proper trash containers such as designated litter barrels at rest areas or other marked locations. Throwing trash into the median, ditches, or anywhere else along the roadway is illegal and dangerous because it can create hazards and harm the environment.

question: When parking uphill next to a curb, what should you do?
options: a: Keep rear tires against the curb.,b: Keep front tires straight.,c: Turn steering wheel away from the curb.
note: When parking uphill with a curb, turn the front wheels away from the curb and let the vehicle roll back slightly until the tire gently touches the curb. If the brakes fail, the curb will stop the vehicle from rolling into traffic.

question: When parking uphill with a curb:
options: a: Keep wheels straight and set the parking brake, b: Turn wheels away from the curb, c: Turn wheels toward the curb
note: When parking uphill with a curb, turn your front wheels away from the curb and set the parking brake. If the brakes fail, the vehicle will roll back slightly and the front tire will rest against the curb, helping prevent it from rolling into traffic.

question: When parking uphill with a curb, what should you do?
options: a: Keep front wheels straight and set the brake.,b: Turn front wheels away from the curb.,c: Turn front wheels toward the curb.
note: When parking uphill with a curb, turn your front wheels away from the curb and let the vehicle roll back slightly until the tire gently touches the curb. This way, if your brakes fail, the curb will stop the car from rolling into traffic.

question: You should not park within ____ of an intersection.
options: a: 20 feet, b: 30 feet, c: 35 feet
note: Many states prohibit parking within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection to keep sight lines clear for drivers and pedestrians. However, specific distances can vary by state law, so always check your local driver handbook for the exact requirement where you are driving.

question: Drive below the posted speed limit when:
options: a: Conditions are less than ideal, b: You see a police car, c: Entering a highway with other cars
note: The posted speed limit applies only when conditions are ideal. In rain, fog, heavy traffic, or other poor conditions, you must slow down below the posted limit so you can stop safely and maintain control of your vehicle.

question: You must not drive faster than:
options: a: The maximum speed limit, b: A speed that’s reasonable and prudent, c: A speed safe for conditions, d: All of the above
note: You must always obey the posted speed limit, but you also must slow down further whenever conditions like rain, fog, traffic, or road work make the posted limit unsafe. The correct speed is the lower of: the posted limit, a speed that is reasonable and prudent, and a speed that is safe for current conditions.

question: What should you do when driving in bad weather?
options: a: Speed up to reach your destination faster., b: Reduce your following distance., c: Increase your following distance.
note: In bad weather, roads can become slippery and it takes longer to stop. You should slow down and increase your following distance so you have more space and time to react if the vehicle ahead brakes or loses control. Reducing your following distance in bad weather is dangerous because it leaves you less room to stop safely.

question: What’s the safest way to drive in traffic?
options: a: Vary your speed to stay alert., b: Drive faster than traffic flow., c: Drive with the flow of traffic within the speed limit.
note: The safest practice is to move with the flow of traffic while staying at or below the posted speed limit. Large speed differences between you and surrounding traffic increase the risk of crashes because other drivers may not anticipate your speed. Never exceed the speed limit, even if other traffic is going faster.

question: What technique helps avoid crashes in icy or snowy conditions?
options: a: Add weight for better traction.,b: Exit highways quickly.,c: Reduce speed and increase following distance.
note: On icy or snowy roads, traction is greatly reduced, so you must drive more slowly and leave much more space between your vehicle and the one ahead. Reducing speed gives you more time to react, and increasing following distance allows for the much longer stopping distances needed on slick surfaces.

question: A “Reduced speed, 35 mph” sign means:
options: a: The 35 mph limit starts at the sign, b: The limit starts at the next speed sign, c: You have time to slow down later
note: A “Reduced speed, 35 mph” sign means the new speed limit begins at the sign. You must be at or below 35 mph when you reach the sign, not some distance after it. Use the distance before the sign to slow down so you are already at the posted speed when you pass it.

question: When should you slow down when exiting a highway?
options: a: On the main road before the exit lane.,b: At a toll booth.,c: After entering the exit lane.
note: On freeways and highways, maintain the main road speed until you are in the exit (deceleration) lane. Once in the exit lane, then slow down to the posted ramp speed. Slowing on the main roadway can surprise drivers behind you and increase the risk of a rear-end collision.

question: A driver traveling much slower than the speed limit:
options: a: Is always a safe driver, b: Always has the right-of-way, c: Should allow following vehicles to pass
note: Driving much slower than the normal flow of traffic can be dangerous because it causes other drivers to brake or change lanes suddenly. If you must drive well below the speed limit on a two-lane road, you should safely pull over or use turnouts where available to let faster vehicles pass.

question: A speed limit represents:
options: a: The maximum or minimum speed you may drive only when conditions are hazardous.,b: The legal maximum (and sometimes minimum) speed for that road under ideal conditions.,c: A suggested speed under ideal conditions.
note: Posted speed limits are set as the legal maximum (and sometimes minimum) speed for a road under ideal conditions. Drivers must still slow down below that speed when conditions are hazardous, such as in bad weather, heavy traffic, or road work zones. They are not just suggestions; they are enforceable limits.

question: Which statement about speed is true?
options: a: Driving too slowly can be dangerous.,b: Speeding can be fatal.,c: Speeding is safe for skilled drivers.
note: Both speeding and driving too slowly can be dangerous. Speeding greatly increases crash severity and stopping distance, but driving much slower than the flow of traffic can also cause sudden braking, tailgating, and risky passing. The statement that speeding is safe for skilled drivers is never true; no level of skill removes the increased risk from excessive speed.

question: When is it illegal to drive below the speed limit?
options: a: When it disrupts traffic flow.,b: In heavy traffic in construction zones.,c: Only in rural areas.
note: Driving significantly below the posted or reasonable speed can be illegal when it unnecessarily interferes with the normal and reasonable movement of traffic. If you must drive slowly for safety (bad weather, mechanical problems, etc.), you should use the right lane when possible and allow faster traffic to pass.

question: What should you do when it starts to sleet or snow while driving?
options: a: Keep windshield and mirrors clear., b: Increase following distance., c: Approach vehicles cautiously., d: All of the above.
note: When it starts to sleet or snow, you should do all three: keep your windshield and mirrors clear for good visibility, increase your following distance to allow more stopping room on slippery roads, and approach other vehicles cautiously to avoid sudden braking or steering that could cause a skid.

question: What should you remember when driving on wet pavement?
options: a: Pavement is slickest just after rain starts.,b: Wet roads can cause hydroplaning.,c: Allow extra space when stopping.,d: All of the above.
note: On wet pavement, the road is often slickest just after the rain starts because oil and residue mix with water, and at higher speeds your tires can hydroplane and lose contact with the road. You should remember all of these hazards and leave extra space for stopping.

question: Which statement is true about driving in changing weather?
options: a: Sudden weather changes require driving adjustments.,b: Slow down in rain and fog.,c: Be aware of vehicles behind you.
note: When weather changes suddenly—such as rain, fog, snow, or strong wind—you must adjust how you drive. This usually means reducing speed, increasing following distance, and being more alert to all surrounding traffic, not just vehicles behind you.

question: What should you do when driving on slippery roads?
options: a: Use alternate routes.,b: Drive as on dry roads.,c: Increase your following distance.
note: On slippery roads, your tires have less grip, so it takes longer to stop. Increasing your following distance gives you more time and space to brake gently and avoid skidding if the vehicle ahead slows or stops suddenly.

question: What’s the minimum following distance when driving over 30 mph?
options: a: One second.,b: Two seconds.,c: Three seconds.
note: Use the three‑second rule as a minimum following distance in good conditions. Pick a fixed object ahead; when the vehicle in front passes it, you should be able to count at least three seconds before you reach the same point. Increase this distance in bad weather, at higher speeds, or when visibility is poor.

question: As you approach an intersection and the light turns from green to yellow, you should:
options: a: Accelerate to beat the red light, b: Brake sharply to stop, c: Slow down and prepare to stop unless already in the intersection
note: A steady yellow light warns that the signal is about to turn red. You should slow down and prepare to stop before the intersection. If you are already in the intersection or too close to stop safely when the light turns yellow, continue through with caution instead of braking hard.

question: A fully loaded tractor-trailer traveling at 55 mph may need up to ____ to stop completely.
options: a: 50 feet, b: 125 feet, c: 400 feet
note: Large trucks need much more distance to stop than passenger cars because of their weight and momentum. A fully loaded tractor‑trailer traveling at about 55 mph can need roughly 400 feet or more to come to a complete stop under good conditions.

question: What does a “Reduced speed, 35 mph” sign mean?
options: a: The 35 mph limit starts at the sign.,b: The limit starts at the next sign.,c: You have time to slow down later.
note: A sign that says “Reduced speed 35 mph” with the 35 inside a speed‑limit style sign means the new 35 mph limit begins at that sign. You are expected to have slowed to that speed by the time you reach the sign and then continue at or below that limit beyond it.

question: To reduce the risk of hydroplaning, you should:
options: a: Avoid speeding on wet roads, b: Use properly inflated tires, c: Replace worn tires, d: All of the above
note: Hydroplaning happens when your tires ride on top of water and lose contact with the road. You reduce this risk by slowing down on wet roads, keeping your tires properly inflated, and replacing tires that have worn or shallow tread so they can channel water away effectively.

question: What speed must you not exceed?
options: a: The maximum speed limit., b: A speed faster than is reasonable and prudent for conditions., c: A speed that is safe for conditions., d: Both a and b.
note: You must never drive faster than the posted maximum speed limit, and you must also slow down further whenever conditions (traffic, weather, visibility, road surface) require it. The law prohibits exceeding the maximum limit and also prohibits any speed that is not reasonable and prudent for conditions.

question: What’s the first response to reduced visibility?
options: a: Turn on headlights., b: Reduce speed., c: Turn on wipers.
note: When visibility is reduced, you should immediately turn on your headlights so you can see and be seen by others. After your lights are on, you should also adjust your speed to match the conditions, but making your vehicle visible is the first priority.

question: Fines for traffic violations in construction and maintenance zones are:
options: a: Reduced, b: Doubled, c: Eliminated
note: In many states, fines for moving violations in construction or maintenance zones are doubled when workers and warning signs are present. Higher fines encourage drivers to slow down and pay extra attention to protect road workers.

question: What should you do when it starts to rain while driving?
options: a: Drive faster than traffic.,b: Drive at the maximum speed limit.,c: Slow down.
note: When it starts to rain, the road becomes especially slippery as water mixes with oil and dirt. You should slow down, increase following distance, and turn on your headlights so you can see and be seen. If visibility becomes too poor or conditions feel unsafe, pull over to a safe area and wait for conditions to improve.

question: To safely drive through a curve:
options: a: Slow down entering, speed up exiting, b: Maintain constant speed, c: Speed up entering, slow down exiting
note: Before entering a curve, reduce your speed so you can stay in your lane and react to hazards. Once you are safely through the sharpest part of the curve and your vehicle is stable, you can gradually accelerate as you exit. Entering too fast makes it easier to lose control or drift out of your lane.

question: At a railroad crossing with no signals or gates, when in a line of traffic:
options: a: You have priority and don’t need to check for trains, b: You may pass slower vehicles, c: Ensure space to cross fully
note: At railroad crossings without signals or gates, you must never enter the tracks unless there is enough room on the far side to clear the tracks completely. This prevents you from being trapped on the tracks if traffic stops.

question: Which is not a factor in a vehicle’s stopping distance?
options: a: Steering ability.,b: Braking distance.,c: Reaction distance.
note: Total stopping distance is the distance your vehicle travels from the moment you see a hazard until you come to a complete stop. It includes perception distance, reaction distance, and braking distance. Steering ability does not change how far it takes you to stop in a straight line.

question: How should you handle turns on slick roads?
options: a: Take turns slower than usual., b: Change lanes quickly., c: Accelerate rapidly.
note: On slick or slippery roads, reduce your speed before entering a turn and take the turn more slowly than usual. Sudden steering, quick lane changes, or rapid acceleration can cause your tires to lose traction and the vehicle to skid.

question: 'Highway hypnosis' results from which driving condition?
options: a: Staring at the road for extended periods, b: Taking frequent breaks, c: Excessive sleep before a trip
note: Highway hypnosis is a trance-like state that can occur on long, monotonous drives when a driver stares straight ahead for too long without actively scanning. The driver may continue to steer and respond but with reduced awareness and slower reactions, increasing crash risk. Taking breaks and being well-rested help prevent it.

question: What increases your vehicle’s stopping distance?
options: a: Wet or icy roads.,b: Paved highways.,c: Driving at night.
note: Wet or icy roads reduce tire traction, so it takes more distance to slow or stop your vehicle. On slippery surfaces you must drive more slowly and leave extra following distance so you can stop safely.

question: Driving while distracted by any activity:
options: a: Is never hazardous, b: Slows reaction to hazards, c: Causes faster driving
note: Any distraction, such as using a phone, eating, or adjusting controls, takes attention away from driving and slows your reaction time. When your reactions are delayed, you are less able to respond quickly to sudden hazards, which greatly increases your risk of a crash.

question: What’s true about driving on a wet roadway?
options: a: Tires are less effective at higher speeds.,b: Good tires negate water’s effects.,c: Deep water is less dangerous.
note: On wet roads, the faster you drive, the harder it is for your tires to squeeze water out of the way and grip the pavement. At higher speeds your tires can ride up on the water (hydroplaning), greatly reducing steering and braking control.

question: What should you be prepared for in a construction zone?
options: a: To stop., b: To change lanes., c: For unexpected worker or equipment movement.
note: Construction zones often have workers and equipment close to moving traffic. You must be prepared for sudden stops, lane shifts, and unexpected movements, and you should slow down and follow all signs and flaggers’ directions.

question: A good defensive driver:
options: a: Always drives slowly, b: Anticipates other drivers’ actions, c: Maintains a constant speed
note: A defensive driver constantly scans the road, anticipates what other drivers, pedestrians, and cyclists might do next, and is ready to react early. This is more important than simply driving slowly or keeping the same speed, because conditions and traffic are always changing.

question: What should you do if your vehicle’s right wheels leave the pavement?
options: a: Stop abruptly.,b: Gradually slow, keep steering straight or parallel to the road, and ease back onto the pavement when safe.,c: Accelerate and steer back quickly.
note: If your right wheels drop off the pavement, stay calm and avoid jerking the wheel back onto the road. Gradually slow down, keep steering straight or parallel to the roadway, and move fully onto the shoulder if needed. When your speed is under control and the lane is clear, gently steer back onto the pavement to avoid skidding or losing control.

question: If you notice a vehicle defect affecting safety, you should:
options: a: Correct it as soon as possible, b: Fix it when affordable, c: Drive slower
note: Any defect that affects the safe operation of your vehicle—such as brakes, tires, lights, or steering—must be corrected as soon as possible. Driving with known safety defects increases your risk of a crash and may be illegal.

question: If the driver ahead is driving with one hand and talking to a passenger, you should:
options: a: Give them extra space, b: Recognize their inattention reduces safety, c: Avoid mimicking their behavior, d: All of the above
note: Inattentive or distracted drivers are more likely to make sudden or unsafe moves. When you see a driver using one hand and focusing on a conversation, you should give them extra space, understand that their reduced attention increases risk, and avoid copying their behavior so you can stay fully focused on the road.

question: Distracted driving is:
options: a: Very rare, b: Extremely dangerous behavior, c: Not a concern
note: Distracted driving is extremely dangerous because it takes your attention away from the road. Looking at a phone, adjusting controls, eating, or any activity that diverts your focus can greatly increase the risk of a crash.

question: What should you do when other drivers are acting aggressively?
options: a: Avoid eye contact., b: Avoid provocative gestures., c: Distance yourself from them., d: All of the above
note: When another driver is aggressive, your goal is to avoid escalating the situation and create space. Do not make eye contact or respond with gestures, and safely slow down, change lanes, or turn off to increase your distance. Using all of these strategies together is the safest response to aggressive driving.

question: When should you drive in a reversible lane with a red X signal?
options: a: If no oncoming traffic is visible.,b: When passing a vehicle.,c: Never.
note: A red X over a lane means that lane is closed to traffic in your direction. You must never drive in a lane showing a red X, even if it appears clear, because traffic may be coming from the opposite direction or the lane may be blocked ahead.

question: Stopping distance increases when stopping:
options: a: On wet or icy roads, b: On paved highways, c: At night
note: On wet or icy roads your tires have less traction, so it takes much longer to stop. You should slow down and increase your following distance whenever the road surface is slippery.

question: To ensure safety when backing your vehicle:
options: a: Honk before shifting to reverse, b: Check behind the vehicle before entering, c: Rely on rearview mirrors
note: Before backing, walk around and check behind your vehicle to be sure there are no children, pedestrians, or obstacles. Then back up slowly while looking over your shoulder and using your mirrors as a supplement, not as your only way of seeing.

question: If an aggressive driver is tailgating you, you should:
options: a: Move out of their way, b: Stare at them while they pass, c: Speed up as they pass
note: If an aggressive driver is tailgating you, the safest response is to move out of their way when it is safe to do so. Change lanes or gradually slow so they can pass. Do not stare at them, gesture, or speed up, as that can escalate the situation and increase crash risk.

question: What should you do on major highways?
options: a: Stay alert., b: Keep your eyes moving., c: Be ready to react to hazards., d: All of the above.
note: On major highways you must do all three: stay alert, keep your eyes moving, and be ready to react to hazards. Good highway driving means constantly scanning ahead, to the sides, and behind you, rather than staring at one spot. This helps you spot problems early and gives you more time and space to react safely.

question: What should you do when meeting a car with blinding headlights?
options: a: Use your high beams until they dim theirs.,b: Briefly flash your headlights and look toward the right edge of your lane.,c: Dim your lights and speed up to pass.
note: When an oncoming driver’s high beams are blinding you, you should dim your own lights and avoid looking directly at the glare by glancing toward the right edge of your lane. You may briefly flash your headlights once to remind the other driver to dim theirs, but never use your high beams continuously or speed up.

question: What should you do when encountering a warning sign?
options: a: Stay aware of surroundings and adjust driving as needed.,b: Ignore the sign if traffic is light.,c: Always reduce speed to 10 mph below the limit.
note: Warning signs alert you to conditions ahead such as curves, intersections, or changes in road surface. When you see a warning sign, you should increase your awareness, scan for hazards, and adjust your driving—often including slowing down—based on what the sign is warning about and the actual conditions.

question: What should you use when driving in fog?
options: a: Parking lights.,b: Low beam headlights.,c: High beam headlights.
note: In fog, always use low beam headlights. High beams reflect off the fog and create glare, making it harder to see. Low beams, and if equipped, fog lights, help you see the road and help others see you without blinding them.

question: What should you do if your wheels slip off the road’s edge?
options: a: Jerk the wheel back onto the pavement.,b: Speed up and steer back gradually.,c: Slow down and ease back onto the pavement.
note: If your wheels drop off the pavement, stay calm, ease off the gas, and slow down gradually. Keep steering straight, then when your speed is under control and the way is clear, gently steer back onto the pavement. Jerking the wheel or speeding up can cause you to lose control or skid into other lanes.

question: What should you do if you notice a vehicle defect affecting safety?
options: a: Correct it as soon as possible.,b: Correct it when affordable.,c: Drive slower.
note: Any defect that affects the safe operation of your vehicle—such as problems with brakes, tires, lights, or steering—should be fixed before driving. Driving with known safety defects increases the risk of a crash and can make you legally responsible if a collision occurs.

question: When driving at night with an oncoming vehicle approaching, your headlights should be:
options: a: On high beam, b: On low beam, c: Off, using parking lights
note: Use low-beam headlights when an oncoming vehicle is within about 500 feet so you do not blind the other driver. High beams can cause glare and make it harder for both of you to see the road safely.

question: If another driver cuts you off in traffic, you should:
options: a: Pull beside them and yell, b: Let it go, c: Flash your high beams
note: Ignoring a driver who cuts you off avoids road rage and maintains safety, preventing dangerous escalations.

question: What is a blind spot in driving?
options: a: An area you can’t see without moving your head.,b: Directly behind your vehicle.,c: Visible in your rearview mirror.
note: A blind spot is any area around your vehicle that you cannot see using your mirrors alone. To check blind spots, you must briefly turn your head and look over your shoulder, especially to the sides and slightly to the rear, before changing lanes or merging.

question: What should you do if your accelerator sticks open while driving?
options: a: Shift to neutral and brake steadily.,b: Slam on your brakes.,c: Turn on your four-way flashers.
note: If the accelerator sticks, keep your eyes on the road, shift to neutral, and apply steady, firm braking while steering to a safe place off the roadway. Once you are safely off the road and stopped, then turn off the ignition. Do not turn the key to the lock position while moving, because you could lose power steering and power brakes.

question: Drowsy drivers:
options: a: Should drink coffee to stay awake, b: May drive as poorly as drunk drivers, c: Can stay alert with open windows and loud radio
note: Drowsy driving slows your reaction time, reduces your awareness, and affects your judgment in ways similar to alcohol. Coffee, loud music, or opening windows may briefly make you feel more awake, but they do not restore full alertness. The only safe solution for serious drowsiness is to rest or change drivers.

question: What should you do when borrowing an unfamiliar vehicle?
options: a: Assume all vehicles are similar., b: Hide your unfamiliarity., c: Check the vehicle and familiarize yourself with its controls before driving.
note: When you drive a vehicle that is new to you, you should first locate and understand the controls such as lights, wipers, turn signals, gear selector, and emergency brake. You should also check for obvious defects like bad tires, nonworking lights, or dirty windows. Knowing how everything works and ensuring the vehicle is in safe condition helps you respond quickly and avoid crashes.

question: Regarding seat belts and child restraints:
options: a: Never place infants in front with airbags, b: Airbags can harm infants in low-speed crashes, c: All passengers must use seat belts or restraints, d: All of the above
note: Infants must never be placed in the front seat with an active airbag because the force of an airbag can seriously injure or kill a child, even in a low-speed crash. All occupants, including children and adults, must use proper seat belts or child safety restraints as required by law to reduce the risk of injury.

question: If an officer is directing traffic at a functioning traffic light, drivers should:
options: a: Follow the traffic light, b: Follow the officer’s directions, c: Honk at the officer
note: When a police officer or other authorized person is directing traffic, their hand signals and directions override traffic lights and signs. You must follow the officer’s instructions, even if they conflict with the signal, to keep traffic moving safely.

question: If an aggressive driver cuts you off, you should:
options: a: Call the police immediately, b: Stay calm and move out of their way, c: Flash your lights to signal their error
note: When another driver is aggressive or cuts you off, focus on safety, not retaliation. Stay calm, give them space, and move out of their way when you can. Avoid eye contact, gestures, or actions that could escalate the situation.

question: If an oncoming vehicle with high beams approaches, you should look toward:
options: a: Either side of the road, b: The center of the road, c: The right side of the road
note: If an oncoming vehicle’s high beams are shining in your eyes, look toward the right side of your lane, using the right edge of the road or the right lane line as a guide. This reduces glare and helps you maintain your lane position until the vehicle passes.

question: Which devices are prohibited on motor vehicles?
options: a: Red flashing lights, b: Radar interference devices, c: Muffler cutouts, d: All of the above
note: Private vehicles may not use red flashing lights, because those are reserved for emergency and certain authorized vehicles. Radar interference devices (radar jammers) are illegal because they interfere with police speed‑enforcement equipment. Muffler cutouts are prohibited because they bypass the muffler, creating excessive noise and violating equipment and noise laws.

question: Your blind spot is the area of the road:
options: a: You cannot see without moving your head, b: Directly behind your vehicle, c: Seen in your rearview mirror
note: Blind spots are areas you cannot see in your mirrors and must turn your head to check. Even with properly adjusted mirrors, there are zones to the sides and slightly behind your vehicle that require a head check before changing lanes or merging.

question: What should small vehicle drivers expect when passing a large vehicle?
options: a: Loud noises.,b: Air pollution.,c: Wind gusts from the large vehicle.
note: When passing a large truck or bus, expect strong wind gusts and air turbulence. These forces can push or pull a smaller vehicle sideways, so keep a firm grip on the steering wheel and be prepared to make small steering corrections while passing.

question: What should you do on slippery roads?
options: a: Drive at the maximum speed limit.,b: Use cruise control for steady speed.,c: Avoid sudden speed or direction changes.
note: On slippery roads, you should slow down and make all changes in speed or direction gradually. Sudden braking, accelerating, or steering can cause your tires to lose grip and the vehicle to skid. Avoid cruise control so you can respond quickly to changing traction.

question: What should concern you most about a low shoulder sign?
options: a: Misaligned headlights due to uneven car height.,b: Tire damage or loss of control from drifting onto the shoulder.,c: Hydroplaning if the shoulder is wet.
note: A LOW SHOULDER sign warns that the edge of the pavement is lower than the adjacent ground, creating a drop‑off. If your tire drifts off the pavement, the height difference can pull the vehicle, damage a tire or wheel, and make it harder to steer back onto the road safely. The main concern is loss of control or damage when a wheel leaves the pavement, not hydroplaning.

question: Which offense causes automatic license suspension?
options: a: Racing on a public road, b: Graffiti, c: Lending a license to another, d: Racing on a public road and lending a license to another
note: Racing on a public road is widely treated as a serious offense and commonly results in automatic license suspension because it greatly endangers others. Graffiti and lending a license can be illegal, but they do not automatically trigger license suspension in all states the way racing or reckless driving often does.

question: Defensive driving means:
options: a: Driving aggressively.,b: Using safe strategies to avoid crashes.,c: Being more hazardous than non-defensive driving.
note: Defensive driving means using safe, proactive strategies—such as scanning ahead, keeping space around your vehicle, and anticipating other drivers’ mistakes—to reduce the risk of crashes, even when conditions or other drivers are not ideal.

question: If a flagger is directing traffic in a construction zone, you must:
options: a: Follow the flagger’s directions, b: Follow surrounding traffic despite the flagger, c: Assume the flagger shouldn’t direct traffic
note: Flaggers in construction or work zones are authorized to control traffic and can override normal traffic signals and signs. You must slow down, be prepared to stop, and follow the flagger’s hand signals and signs to protect both workers and drivers.

question: What should you do when driving on an interstate?
options: a: Stop on the shoulder if tired.,b: Always use cruise control.,c: Signal and check mirrors and blind spots before changing lanes.
note: On interstates, you must always signal and check mirrors and blind spots before changing lanes. Cruise control is optional and not always safe (e.g., in heavy traffic or bad weather), and you should only stop on the shoulder for emergencies, not just because you feel a little tired.

question: What should you do when nearing an accident scene?
options: a: Focus on driving.,b: Keep moving.,c: Stop if involved or help is needed.
note: If you come upon an accident, you should only stop if you are directly involved or if emergency help has not yet arrived and your assistance is needed. Otherwise, continue driving carefully so you do not block traffic or interfere with emergency responders.

question: What should you do when encountering an aggressive driver?
options: a: Avoid eye contact and let them pass.,b: Cut them off to slow them down.,c: Tailgate them in retaliation.
note: If you encounter an aggressive driver, stay calm, do not make eye contact or respond with gestures, and safely let them pass. Creating distance between your vehicle and the aggressive driver reduces the chance of a crash or confrontation.

question: When seeing angry drivers around you:
options: a: Avoid eye contact, b: Avoid provocative gestures, c: Distance yourself from them, d: All of the above
note: Avoiding eye contact and gestures and creating distance from angry drivers helps prevent road rage from escalating. Staying calm and not engaging gives you more time and space to react safely if the other driver behaves unpredictably.

question: Which must you obey above all others?
options: a: A steady red light, b: A police officer, c: A stop sign
note: You must always obey a police officer’s directions, even if they conflict with traffic lights or signs. Officers can override normal traffic controls to manage emergencies, collisions, or special situations, and their instructions take priority for safety.

question: What should you know about sharing the road with trucks?
options: a: Trucks need longer stopping distances.,b: Trucks pass faster on downgrades.,c: Trucks have a smaller turning radius.
note: Large trucks are much heavier than passenger cars and need a longer distance to stop. Leave extra following distance and avoid cutting in front of trucks so they have enough space to brake safely.

question: What’s the minimum following distance when driving under 30 mph?
options: a: One second.,b: Two seconds.,c: Three seconds.
note: A two‑second following distance at speeds under about 30 mph is a widely taught minimum. It gives you basic time to see a problem and begin braking. In bad weather, heavy traffic, or at higher speeds, you should increase this to three or more seconds for extra safety.

question: If another vehicle risks hitting you, you should:
options: a: Sound your horn, b: Wave your arms, c: Use your emergency lights
note: If another vehicle may hit you, use your horn to warn the other driver and draw attention to your vehicle. A quick, loud horn signal is the standard way to alert others to prevent a collision.

question: What should you do when passing a recently parked vehicle?
options: a: Assume the driver may open the door.,b: Speed up.,c: Brake hard.
note: When passing a recently parked or stopped vehicle, you should assume someone might open a door or pull out suddenly. Slow slightly if needed, leave extra space, and be prepared to brake or steer smoothly to avoid a door or sudden movement into your path.

question: What should you know when approaching a heavy truck from behind on a hill?
options: a: The truck may be slower than the speed limit., b: You can always safely pass it., c: You can always legally pass it.
note: Heavy trucks often slow down on hills because of their weight and engine limits, so they may travel below the speed limit on upgrades. When approaching a truck from behind on a hill, expect it to be slower, allow extra following distance, and only pass if it is legal and you have clear visibility and enough space to complete the pass safely.

question: When approaching a heavy truck from behind on a hill, you should know:
options: a: The truck may be slower than the speed limit, b: You may not safely pass, c: Passing is illegal, d: All of the above
note: When you approach a heavy truck from behind on a hill, you must assume that passing may not be safe. Trucks often move slowly uphill, and hills limit your ability to see oncoming traffic, making passing risky. Passing is not automatically illegal, but it is frequently unsafe or prohibited where visibility is limited.

question: Defensive driving involves:
options: a: Identifying and avoiding dangerous situations, b: Getting ahead of poor drivers, c: Following closely behind other vehicles
note: Defensive driving means staying alert, anticipating potential hazards, and adjusting your driving early to avoid collisions. This includes keeping safe following distances, watching for mistakes by other drivers, and having an escape plan.

question: What should you do if your tire blows out while driving?
options: a: Slam on brakes.,b: Hold the wheel tightly and slow to a stop.,c: Keep driving normally.
note: When a tire blows out, hold the steering wheel firmly to keep control, ease your foot off the accelerator, and let the vehicle slow down gradually. Once you have slowed and are in control, gently brake and steer to a safe place off the road. Slamming on the brakes can cause you to lose control, especially at higher speeds.

question: A space cushion around your vehicle is important because it:
options: a: Prevents distractions from other vehicles, b: Gives you time to react to sudden situations, c: Maintains safe traffic flow
note: Keeping a space cushion in front, behind, and to the sides of your vehicle gives you room and time to brake, change lanes, or steer away from sudden hazards. Extra space reduces the chance of rear-end collisions and allows smoother, safer driving decisions.

question: What should you do when driving in rain?
options: a: Use low beam headlights.,b: Use high beam headlights.,c: Use parking lights.
note: In rain, you should turn on your low beam headlights so you can see the road and so other drivers can see you. High beams reflect off rain and can cause glare, making it harder to see. Parking lights alone are not sufficient and are generally illegal to use as a substitute for headlights in poor visibility.

question: When approaching a railroad crossing without signals or gates, you should:
options: a: Cross quickly, b: Always stop, c: Yield to any train
note: At a railroad crossing without lights or gates, you must slow down, look, and listen for trains and be prepared to stop. Trains always have the right of way, so you must yield to any approaching train and only cross when you are sure it is safe and the tracks are clear.

question: What should you do when a driver behind you wants to pass?
options: a: Speed up., b: Maintain a steady speed., c: Slow slightly to allow more room to pass safely.
note: When another driver wants to pass you, you should help them do it safely. Maintain a steady speed or slightly slow down to create more space in front of you so the passing driver has enough room to move back into the lane without cutting too closely in front of you.

question: Which is not a factor in stopping distance?
options: a: Steering ability, b: Braking distance, c: Reaction distance
note: Total stopping distance is made up of perception distance (seeing the hazard), reaction distance (moving your foot to the brake), and braking distance (the car slowing to a stop). Steering ability does not change how far the vehicle travels before it stops.

question: On a wet roadway:
options: a: Faster driving reduces tire effectiveness, b: Water doesn’t affect good tires, c: Deep water is less dangerous than shallow
note: On a wet roadway, increasing speed makes it easier for your tires to lose contact with the road surface. This loss of traction, called hydroplaning, can cause you to lose steering and braking control, so you should slow down when the road is wet.

question: If a tire blows out while driving, you should:
options: a: Brake hard immediately, b: Steer straight and slow gradually, c: Maintain speed and steer straight
note: If a tire blows out, hold the steering wheel firmly, keep the vehicle going straight, and ease off the accelerator. Let the car slow down gradually, then apply the brakes gently once you have control and can pull off the road safely. Hard braking or sudden steering can cause you to lose control.

question: Your first response to reduced visibility should be:
options: a: Turning on headlights, b: Reducing speed, c: Turning on windshield wipers
note: Reducing speed is the safest first reaction when visibility drops (fog, heavy rain, snow, smoke, glare). Slowing down gives you more time to see hazards and stop safely. After slowing, you should also use headlights and wipers as needed, but speed reduction is the primary immediate response.

question: At dusk or on cloudy days, you should:
options: a: Use four-way flashers.,b: Use parking lights.,c: Turn on your headlights.
note: Headlights should be turned on at dusk, in rain, fog, or on cloudy days so that you can see and be seen. Use low beams when other vehicles are nearby to avoid blinding other drivers.

question: As your speed increases, your field of vision:
options: a: Expands, b: Narrows, c: Remains unchanged
note: As speed increases, your field of vision narrows, meaning you see less to the sides and focus more straight ahead. This “tunnel vision” effect makes it easier to miss hazards at the edges of the road, so you must scan more actively and adjust your speed to conditions.

question: What should you do if your power steering fails while driving?
options: a: Honk and turn off the ignition.,b: Turn on hazard lights and continue driving normally.,c: Steer harder, reduce speed, signal or use hazard lights if needed, and pull off to a safe place to stop.
note: If power steering fails, the vehicle will still steer, but it will take much more effort. Keep a firm grip on the wheel, gradually reduce your speed, signal and turn on your hazard lights if needed, and carefully move to a safe place off the road. Do not turn off the ignition while moving, because that can lock the steering wheel and disable power brakes.

question: Drivers should use low beam headlights:
options: a: In fog, dust, or rain, b: When closely following another vehicle at night, c: Within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle at night, d: All of the above
note: Low beam headlights are safer in fog, dust, and rain because high beams reflect off moisture and reduce visibility. At night, you should use low beams when following another vehicle closely or when an oncoming vehicle is within about 500 feet so you do not blind other drivers.

question: At night, it is most difficult to see:
options: a: Road signs, b: Pedestrians, c: Other vehicles
note: Pedestrians are the hardest to see at night because they are smaller, often wear dark clothing, and do not have lights like vehicles or the reflective surfaces that road signs have. Always scan carefully for people walking along the road or crossing, especially in poorly lit areas.

question: A seat belt should be adjusted to:
options: a: Be loose, b: Fit snugly across your hips and lower abdomen, c: Be hidden under the seat
note: The lap belt should fit snugly across your hips and low on the abdomen, not across the stomach, and the shoulder belt should cross the chest and shoulder without cutting into the neck. A snug, low fit helps the belt hold your body against the stronger bones of the pelvis in a crash.

question: What should you do when approaching a roundabout?
options: a: Increase your speed.,b: Maintain your speed.,c: Slow down to a safe speed and be prepared to stop if necessary.
note: When approaching a roundabout, you should slow down to a safe speed, look for pedestrians and traffic already in the circle, and yield to traffic in the roundabout. You usually do not stop unless traffic conditions require it.

question: What’s the first thing to adjust when preparing to drive?
options: a: Your seat belt.,b: Your seat.,c: Your rearview mirror.
note: When preparing to drive, adjust your seat first so you can reach the pedals and controls comfortably and see clearly over the dashboard. Next, adjust the steering wheel to a safe, comfortable position, and then set your mirrors. Seat belts are fastened after you are properly seated and adjusted.

question: When driving in sleet or snow, you should:
options: a: Keep windshield and mirrors clear, b: Increase following distance, c: Approach vehicles cautiously, d: All of the above
note: In sleet or snow, keep your windshield and mirrors clear for visibility, increase your following distance because stopping takes longer, and approach other vehicles cautiously to avoid skids and collisions.

question: What’s a safe way to drive through a curve?
options: a: Slow down entering, speed up exiting.,b: Maintain constant speed.,c: Speed up entering, slow down exiting.
note: Before entering a curve, slow down so you can maintain control and stay in your lane. As you move through and see the road ahead clearly, you can gradually accelerate when exiting the curve if conditions are safe.

question: What should you do if your accelerator sticks while driving?
options: a: Try to pull it up manually.,b: Shift to park.,c: Shift to neutral and brake steadily.
note: If the accelerator sticks, shift to neutral to disconnect engine power from the wheels, then apply the brakes steadily and steer to a safe place off the road. Do not turn the ignition off while moving, and do not shift into park until the vehicle is fully stopped.

question: At a double railroad crossing:
options: a: Proceed after one train passes, b: Always stop before crossing, c: Check for another train after one passes
note: At a double railroad crossing, one train may hide another coming from the opposite direction or on another track. After the first train passes, wait until you have a clear view of all tracks in both directions and actively look and listen for another train before crossing.

question: To combat 'Highway hypnosis', drivers should:
options: a: Scan the road actively, b: Stop every 100 miles, c: Limit driving to eight hours daily, d: All of the above
note: Highway hypnosis is best prevented by staying mentally engaged with the driving task, especially by actively scanning the road ahead, checking mirrors, and looking around for potential hazards. While taking regular breaks and limiting long stretches of driving are good safety habits, there is no fixed legal requirement such as exactly every 100 miles or a maximum of eight hours per day. The key technique is to keep your eyes and mind moving so you do not become drowsy or fall into a trance-like state.

question: Car drivers should be aware that large trucks:
options: a: Have large blind spots, b: Stop more quickly than cars, c: Need less room to maneuver
note: Large trucks have big blind spots on all four sides, especially directly behind and along each side. If you cannot see the truck driver’s mirrors, the driver likely cannot see you. Avoid lingering in these blind spots and give trucks extra space to turn and change lanes.

question: What might a flag on a bicycle’s rear indicate?
options: a: To increase the rider’s visibility to drivers.,b: The rider exceeds the speed limit.,c: The rider may be hearing impaired.
note: A flag on the rear of a bicycle is generally used to make the rider more visible to drivers, especially when the rider is small or when traffic and parked vehicles might block the view. Regardless of why the flag is there, you should always slow down, give bicyclists plenty of space, and pass only when it is safe. A hearing‑impaired cyclist is more commonly identified by a specific symbol or sign rather than just a flag.

question: If an approaching driver fails to dim their high beams, you should look toward:
options: a: The wheels of the approaching vehicle, b: The right side of the road, c: The left side of the road
note: When an oncoming driver does not dim their high beams, looking slightly toward the right edge of your lane helps you avoid being blinded while still keeping track of your lane position. Do not stare into the bright lights, and check the road ahead with quick glances to stay safely centered in your lane.

question: Which statement is true?
options: a: Sudden weather changes require driving adjustments, b: Slow down in rain and fog, c: Be aware of vehicles behind in bad weather, d: All of the above
note: In bad weather you must adjust your driving: slow down for reduced visibility and traction, and stay aware of vehicles behind and around you. All of the listed statements are correct, so the best choice is the one that includes all of them.

question: How does driving at 60 mph affect your field of vision?
options: a: Reduced to about two-thirds of your stationary field of vision., b: Reduced to one-fifth of stationary vision., c: Reduced to three-fifths of stationary vision.
note: As speed increases, your field of vision narrows, a phenomenon sometimes called "tunnel vision." At highway speeds around 55–60 mph, you see much less to the sides than when you are stopped, which makes it easier to miss hazards such as pedestrians, bicyclists, or vehicles entering from side streets. Because of this reduced side vision, you must scan more deliberately and avoid driving faster than conditions safely allow.

question: What should drivers consider when near heavy trucks?
options: a: Trucks need longer stopping distances.,b: Trucks stop faster than smaller vehicles.,c: Trucks are quieter than smaller vehicles.
note: Large trucks are heavier and need more distance to stop than smaller vehicles. When driving near trucks, avoid cutting in front of them and leave extra space so they have enough room to slow or stop safely.

question: What should your headlights be set to when driving at night with an oncoming vehicle?
options: a: High beam.,b: Low beam.,c: Parking lights.
note: Use low beam headlights when an oncoming vehicle is approaching so you do not blind the other driver. High beams can cause glare and make it hard for them to see the road. Switch to low beams whenever you are within about 500 feet of oncoming traffic or when following another vehicle closely.

question: When driving in fog, you should:
options: a: Drive cautiously at reduced speed, b: Avoid high beam headlights, c: Use low beam headlights, d: All of the above
note: In fog, visibility is reduced and light reflects off water droplets. You should slow down, use low beam headlights so the light stays on the road, and avoid high beams because they create glare and make it harder to see.

question: What lights should you use when driving in fog?
options: a: Low beam headlights.,b: High beam headlights.,c: Parking lights.
note: In fog, use low beam headlights so the light aims down at the road. High beams reflect off the water droplets in the fog and shine back into your eyes, making it harder to see. Parking lights alone are not enough for you to see or be seen.

question: Which statement about winter driving is false?
options: a: Winter is the most challenging driving season, b: Check antifreeze and washer fluid levels, c: Using cruise control is safe in winter
note: On snow, ice, or other slippery winter surfaces, you should not use cruise control. Cruise control can cause your wheels to spin or lose traction because it tries to maintain speed even when the road is slick. Winter is indeed one of the most challenging driving seasons, and checking antifreeze and washer fluid is an important safety step.

question: What should you do when driving to an unfamiliar area?
options: a: Rely on road signs.,b: Plan your trip in advance.,c: Know only the general destination.
note: Before driving into an unfamiliar area, plan your route in advance using a map, GPS, or directions. This reduces last‑second lane changes, sudden stops, and missed turns, helping you drive more safely and pay better attention to traffic and road conditions.

question: What should drivers do with an Anti-Lock Braking System (ABS) when losing traction on a slippery road?
options: a: Pump the brakes.,b: Press and hold the brake pedal.,c: Press and hold the gas pedal.
note: With ABS, you should press the brake pedal firmly and hold it. The system automatically pumps the brakes to help prevent wheel lockup and maintain steering control on slippery surfaces. Do not pump the brakes yourself when your vehicle has ABS.

section-name: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability
question: A telltale sign of an intoxicated driver is:
options: a: Weaving between lanes, b: Driving slower than traffic flow, c: Making abrupt stops, d: All of the above
note: Weaving between lanes, driving noticeably slower than the normal flow of traffic, and making abrupt or unnecessary stops are all common signs of an impaired driver. Alcohol and drugs reduce coordination, judgment, and reaction time, which often shows up as poor lane control, inconsistent speed, and sudden, unsafe maneuvers.
handbook-section: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability

section-name: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability
question: To overcome the effects of alcohol consumption, you need:
options: a: Tomato juice and lime, b: Hot coffee, c: Time
note: Only time allows the body to metabolize and eliminate alcohol, restoring normal driving ability.
handbook-section: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability

section-name: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability
question: Your body eliminates approximately:
options: a: Three alcoholic drinks per hour, b: One alcoholic drink per hour, c: Two alcoholic drinks per hour
note: On average, the body can process about one standard drink per hour, though this rate varies with body size, sex, health, and other factors. Because you cannot speed up this process by coffee, cold showers, or exercise, the only safe choice is to give yourself plenty of time or avoid drinking if you plan to drive.
handbook-section: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability

section-name: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability
question: Which medications can affect driving ability?
options: a: Any medication, b: Only headache medicine, c: Only diet pills
note: Many medications—prescription, over‑the‑counter, and even some herbal products—can cause drowsiness, blurred vision, slowed reaction time, or other side effects that make driving unsafe. Always read the label and warnings, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if it is safe to drive when taking any medication.
handbook-section: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability

section-name: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability
question: A driver’s ability to operate a vehicle can be impaired by:
options: a: Alcohol, b: Any medication, c: Lack of sleep, d: All of the above
note: Alcohol slows reaction time and judgment, many medications can cause drowsiness or affect coordination, and lack of sleep leads to fatigue and slower responses. Any of these can seriously impair your ability to drive safely, so you must be cautious with alcohol, read medication labels, and avoid driving when tired.
handbook-section: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability

section-name: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability
question: Alcohol consumption negatively affects:
options: a: Judgment, b: Reasoning ability, c: Vision, d: All of the above
note: Alcohol reduces your ability to judge situations, think clearly, and see hazards. It impairs judgment, slows reasoning and decision‑making, and can blur or narrow your vision, all of which greatly increase crash risk.
handbook-section: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability

section-name: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability
question: Which medications might affect driving ability?
options: a: Any medication.,b: Only headache medicine.,c: Only diet pills.
note: Any medication, including prescriptions, over‑the‑counter drugs, and herbal products, can affect your ability to drive safely. Some may cause drowsiness, blurred vision, or slower reaction time. Always read warning labels and, when in doubt, ask a doctor or pharmacist before driving.
handbook-section: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability

section-name: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability
question: Drivers who consume alcohol before driving:
options: a: Are fully aware of risks, b: Lack sufficient control over body and vehicle, c: Are better drivers due to caution
